title: Reading Mark

objectives.can: Read Markan narrative: καὶ εὐθύς, the historical present, the imperfect, and parataxis.

explanation.summary: Mark tells its story in plain, fast-moving Greek: clause after clause joined by καί, the word εὐθύς again and again, and a mixture of present and imperfect tenses for past events. Once you know these habits, a page of Mark reads quickly.

sections.heading: Clause after clause: parataxis with καί
body: Grammarians describe Mark's narrative as largely paratactic: short clauses set side by side, most of them opening with καί. In Mark 1:18 a whole small scene is one sentence that begins with καί. In 1:21–28 almost every verse begins with καί too.

Read Mark verse by verse and watch what changes between one καί and the next: a new subject, a new place, a new action. Often the only thing that tells you a new episode has begun is a new subject or place, because καί is so common that it carries very little meaning on its own.

sections.heading: εὐθύς: 'at once'
body: The word εὐθύς is a favourite of Mark's: it appears again and again, usually after καί, as in καὶ εὐθύς in 1:18, 1:21, 1:23. In these places it is not an adjective describing a noun but an adverb, 'at once, straight away', and it keeps the story moving. (The corpus tags the form as an adjective, because the word is an adjective in origin, but in Mark it is used as an adverb.)

Commentators note that Mark uses it much more often than Matthew or Luke do. Its force is often weak: it is the narrator's way of hurrying on, not always a claim that something happened that very second. Translate it, or leave it out, according to what the sentence needs.

sections.heading: Present and imperfect in the story
body: Mark moves between past tenses and the present tense inside one narrative. In 1:21 the verse opens with εἰσπορεύονται, a present tense, for something that happened in the past, and the next clause goes on with ἐδίδασκεν, an imperfect. The first is called the historical present: it presents a past event as if the reader were watching it. In 1:37 the aorist εὗρον is followed by the present λέγουσιν. Translate such presents by the past in English, as the context asks.

The imperfect usually describes what was going on or was repeated: ἐδίδασκεν, 'he was teaching', in 1:21 and ἐξεπλήσσοντο, 'they were astonished', in 1:22. It sets the background to a scene, and the aorist then reports the events that come out of it, as in the aorist ἀνέκραξεν, 'he cried out', in 1:23. Do not read the imperfect as a mechanical English 'was -ing' every time; ask what the narrator is doing with the scene.

sections.heading: Participles, γάρ and quoted speech
body: Mark piles participles onto a main verb with καί. In 1:26 the unclean spirit does three things: the two aorist participles σπαράξαν and φωνῆσαν lead to the main verb ἐξῆλθεν, 'came out'. Find the finite verb first, then see how each participle fits.

Mark also uses an explanatory γάρ clause to give the background: in 1:22 ἦν γὰρ διδάσκων αὐτούς gives the reason for their astonishment. The verb ἦν with the participle διδάσκων is a periphrastic imperfect, 'he was teaching'.
Speech often arrives with ὅτι, which here does the work of quotation marks: in 1:37 λέγουσιν αὐτῷ ὅτι Πάντες ζητοῦσίν σε. Do not translate ὅτι as 'because' here.

sections.heading: How to read the passage
body: Read Mark 1:21–28 once for the story: a sabbath in the synagogue at Capernaum, teaching, a man with an unclean spirit, a command, and the news spreading. Then read it again clause by clause. At each καί ask what is new. At each present tense ask whether it is a historical present, and at each imperfect ask what scene it paints.

misunderstandings: Reading every εὐθύς as 'immediately' with a stopwatch. It is often just a narrator's connective, and it is an adverb here even though the word has adjective endings.
Reading a historical present such as εἰσπορεύονται as an event happening now. It belongs to the past story.
Treating every καί as 'and' with a strong link. In Mark καί often just begins the next step of the story, and the real connection has to be read from the context.
Taking ὅτι after λέγουσιν as 'because'. It introduces what was said.

deeper.heading: Why Mark sounds the way it does
body: Readers have long noticed that Mark's Greek is plainer than Luke's and shares features with ordinary spoken Greek of its time, and also with Semitic patterns of narrative such as the string of clauses joined by 'and'. Scholars weigh these influences differently, and the grammar can describe the habits but cannot settle where they came from.

options: It is over and has no connection to the teaching
It went on, or was repeated, while he taught
It is a command to the crowd

options: None of them is a present tense

options: Do you know who I am?

options: ἡ ἀκοή: the report about him
check.explain: ἡ ἀκοὴ αὐτοῦ is the nominative. αὐτοῦ is genitive, 'of him', and the whole verse says that the report about him went out at once everywhere.

reading.why: Eight verses that show Markan narrative at work: nearly every verse opens with καί, εὐθύς returns, a historical present opens the scene, imperfects set it, and participles pile up before the main verb.
